extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners as secondary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for examining whether claimed inventions satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 101 — i.e., whether claims fall into statutory categories and are not directed to judicial exceptions (or, if they are, whether they recite 'significantly more'). Provides the Alice/Mayo two-part test, claim construction (BRI) instructions, pathways for eligibility, and procedures for formulating rejections and evaluating responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories. Second, the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the four statutory categories (processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter) and identifies judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena). Cites Alice/Mayo framework as the controlling two-part test and instructs that the Alice/Mayo test is the only test that should be used. Advises examiners to consult MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.05 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category requirement (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must fall within one or more of the four statutory categories enumerated in 35 U.S.C. 101: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'process' as a series of acts; explains machines/manufactures/compositions as physical/tangible things. For non-process categories, the claimed subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. If a claim's Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) covers non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim prior to examining for eligibility, because BRI sets the boundaries of coverage and affects whether claims are statutory or encompass exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction affects both Step 1 and the Alice/Mayo analysis (Step 2A and 2B). If BRI embraces both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim as a whole is non-statutory. Best practice: point out BRI and recommend applicant amendment when appropriate. See MPEP § 2111 for more on BRI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2: Determine judicial exception and 'significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A: Determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon). Step 2B: If so, determine whether additional elements individually or in combination provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the controlling framework; courts call the second part the search for an 'inventive concept.' Machine-or-transformation and other clues should be considered as part of the integration/'significantly more' determination, not as separate tests. See MPEP §§ 2106.04 and 2106.05 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways A/B/C for streamlined eligibility evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Three pathways to eligibility: Pathway A (self-evident eligibility/streamlined), Pathway B (claim falls within statutory category and is not directed to a judicial exception), Pathway C (claim is directed to a judicial exception but recites additional elements that amount to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner is uncertain whether streamlined analysis applies, conduct full eligibility analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. See MPEP § 2106.06 for streamlined analysis rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of non-statutory product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples include products that do not have a physical or tangible form (e.g., 'data per se' or 'software per se'), transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., propagating carrier waves), and subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains software expressed as code or instructions detached from any medium is intangible; transitory signals lack concrete structure; product claims must have physical/tangible form to satisfy Step 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: If BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments → reject under Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces non-statutory subject matter and therefore fails Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: point out BRI and recommend claim narrowing amendment. Use specified form paragraphs when making Step 1 rejections (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)(1)). Example: 'machine-readable medium' claims that encompass carrier waves can be non-statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions defined (abstract ideas; laws of nature; natural phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions are subject matter courts have found outside the statutory categories: abstract ideas (e.g., mathematical formulas, mental processes), laws of nature, and natural phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting Supreme Court concern that monopolization of these basic tools may impede innovation, but also that claims involving such exceptions aren't ineligible just because they involve them — eligibility depends on application/integration. See cases cited (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Determine whether claim is directed to an abstract idea (groupings and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the claim recites an abstract idea by reference to example categories and groupings of abstract ideas (including mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP contains example lists and 'tentative abstract ideas' — examiners should use these groupings to analyze whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea and consult subsection 2106.04(a) for examples and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a product has 'markedly different characteristics' from a naturally occurring product such that it is not merely a natural product or phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used when assessing laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature — to determine whether claimed subject matter is significantly different from what occurs in nature (see MPEP § 2106.04(b)/(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A prong two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application — i.e., whether the claim applies the exception in a way that imposes a meaningful limitation, ties it to a particular machine, transforms an article, or achieves a technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the exception is integrated into a practical application, the claim may be eligible at Step 2A (no need to go to Step 2B). See MPEP § 2106.04(d) and subsections for guidance on evaluating 'integration' (including improvements to computer functionality, particular treatment/prophylaxis, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Whether claim recites additional elements amounting to 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are directed to a judicial exception, evaluate whether additional elements, individually or in ordered combination, provide 'significantly more' than the exception (i.e., an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2106.05 lists categories and examples of what can constitute significantly more (improvements to computer/technology, particular machine, particular transformation, meaningful limitations, etc.) and what typically does not (well-understood, routine, conventional activity; mere instructions to apply the exception; insignificant extra-solution activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology (Step 2A prong two and Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that improve computer functionality or other technology/technical fields can show integration into a practical application (Step 2A) or can supply 'significantly more' at Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim provides an unconventional technical solution to a technological problem or improves computer operation (see Enfish, McRO examples). Use this as a strong indicator of eligibility when adequately claimed/constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine (Step 2B(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is tied to a particular machine can provide 'significantly more' than an abstract idea or other judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the machine limitation is more than a generic computer or conventional hardware; mere recitation of a computer is often insufficient unless it is a particular machine that imposes meaningful limits on the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation (Step 2B(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A transformation of an article to a different state or thing (the 'particular transformation' test) can supply 'significantly more' and support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claimed process effects a transformation of a specific article and whether that transformation is central to the claim's eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (negative factor in Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely recite well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously known in the field do not supply 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify whether additional claim elements are well-known and conventional at the time of the claim. If so, such elements are unlikely to convert a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter (see MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (negative factor in Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that amount to mere instructions to apply an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (e.g., 'apply this algorithm' or 'perform these mental steps') do not provide 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between meaningful application/implementation and mere steps of using the exception. 'Mere instructions' and 'insignificant extra-solution activity' are common pitfalls leading to ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity that is insignificant to the solution of a technical problem — e.g., token data-gathering steps, generic post-solution activity, or conventional data storage — does not render a claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claimed non-exception elements are integral to solving a technological problem or are merely post-hoc or conventional add-ons (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations and field-of-use considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Other claimed limitations — including particular techniques, data structures, or particular fields of use/technological environments — may be evaluated for whether they meaningfully limit the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abstract idea does not become nonabstract by limiting to a particular field of use or technological environment alone; however, meaningful limitations that impose technical improvements may support eligibility (see MPEP §§ 2106.05(e) and 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis: eligibility is self-evident or clear technology improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When eligibility of a claim is self-evident (Pathway A) or there is a clear improvement to technology or computer functionality (2106.06(b)), a streamlined analysis may be used to find the claim eligible without full two-part analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should use streamlined analysis only when appropriate for examination efficiency and consistency; if uncertain, perform the full Alice/Mayo two-part analysis. If a claim could be eligible under Pathway A but is analyzed further, it will be found eligible under Pathway B or C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting for lack of subject matter eligibility, examiners must use appropriate form paragraphs and support the rejection with explanation tying claim limitations to the basis for ineligibility; see MPEP § 2106.07.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2106.07(a)(1) identifies form paragraphs for § 101 rejections. 2106.07(b) instructs how to evaluate applicant responses; 2106.07(c) discusses clarifying the record. Rejections should explain BRI, the judicial exception identified, why the claim is directed to the exception, and why any additional elements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must still consider other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is only a threshold inquiry. Even if an invention is eligible under § 101, the claim must satisfy novelty (102), nonobviousness (103), written description/enablement/definiteness (112), utility, inventorship, and double patenting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP reminds examiners to continue complete examination under all applicable statutes and not to conflate § 101 eligibility with other requirements. Use MPEP § 2103 and relevant subsequent chapters for these analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant's responses and clarifying the record
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant responds to a § 101 rejection, examiners should evaluate arguments and evidence in view of the Alice/Mayo framework and update the record, requesting clarification or additional claim amendments if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2106.07(b) and (c) provide procedural considerations for evaluating responses and maintaining clear prosecution history. Examiner should articulate reasons for sustaining or withdrawing rejections and advise on amendment strategies.
